items.note: Central Indian sculpture of the 10th-13th centuries under the Chandellas and Paramaras of Dhara blends east Indian and Rajputana-Gujarat traditions
The Paramara sculptural tradition is stored at Dhara and Mandsor in Indore and Gwalior

Paramara art prolific in sculpture but hardly reached high aesthetic achievement; products belong to the Rajputana idiom; Bhoja (c. A.D. 1000-1055) the greatest builder and lover of art of the dynasty
Sarasvati image at Dhara shows Paramara sculpture at its best; other specimens at Mandu, Dhar museum, the walls of the Nilakantha or Udayesvara temple at Udayapur, Ujjain and Indore
Paramara figures are largely conceived in ample dimensions, informed by classical form but with blank, uninspired faces

Under some Tantric influence Bhoja expanded the canon for depicting mithunas in his Samarangana-Sutradhara (XXXIV, 33-34); the woman fully engaged in love-play, the lover if desired shown eager for sport with slightly slender body
items.gloss: The woman is intent on love-play; the lover, at will, should be shown eager for sexual sport with somewhat slender limbs.

items.note: Samaranganasutradhara, Aparajitaprccha and Manasollasa deal in detail with icons of different cults and with materials, mudras, ornament, drapery and weapons
Samaranganasutradhara lists twenty merits and twenty demerits of an image
Aparajitaprccha describes anthropomorphic forms of Siva including Nandisvara, Candranatha, eleven Rudras, Sadyojata, Ganesa, Umamahesvara, Ardhanarisvara, Harihara and dikpalas
Samaranganasutradhara devotes three chapters to mudralogy: hand poses, body poses (sthanas) and standing postures of the legs
Samaranganasutradhara expounds the weapons of Kartikeya, such as sword, club, shield and bow
Aparajitaprccha lists sixteen ornaments that frequently appear in the sculptures of the Paramaras, Chandellas and Gahadvalas
According to the Samaranganasutradhara the sculptor's supreme achievement is aesthetic bhava-vyakti, giving the image a distinct character
Samaranganasutradhara describes Brahma with pot-belly, clotted hair and long moustache or beard; the Aparajitaprccha also gives him a beard
Samaranganasutradhara lays down that the Visnu image be vaidurya-coloured and wear yellow garments
Samaranganasutradhara devotes a chapter to the substances of lingas (earth, metals, gems, timber, stone) and classifies them by measurement relative to temple and worshipper, material and potency
Two types of Siva icon are found, the linga and the human form; the linga is associated with Mahesvara and, per Aparajita-precha, typifies Siva and Sakti as a cosmic emblem
The mild form of Siva shown with clotted hair shining with the moon, blue neck (Nilakantha) and an extraordinary crown

Nrta murtis of dancing Siva: a separate place is given to Nataraja in each important temple; examples include the Nartesvara dancing on a bull and the bhadra niches of Kandariya and Muladeva at Khajuraho
In north Indian temples Nandi is a squatted bull on a raised pedestal facing the entrance of practically every Saiva shrine
Samaranganasutradhara elaborates the figure of Kartikeya like the morning sun, youthful, with six heads or one, and more hands in town temples than village ones
Samaranganasutradhara describes Sri as a youthful figure with full-moon face, white complexion and white garment, lotus in right hand, bathed by two elephants
By Bhoja's orders the sculptor Manathala executed a Sarasvati image now in the British Museum
O.C. Ganguly praises the Bhoja Sarasvati as a chef-d'oeuvre of rare beauty in serenity of pose, rhythm and restrained treatment of anatomy
Sivaramamurti: one of the most marvellous creations of the sculptor of the Paramara realm patronised by Bhoja, resembling the Pratihara school and the idiom of Gujarat
Pedestal inscription dated A.D. 1035 (Samvat 1091), translated by K.N. Dikshit: Bhoja, moon among kings, had the auspicious image made by Manathala, son of the craftsman Sahira, written by Sivadeva
Samarangana sutradhara devotes several chapters to painting, dealing with rasas, rasadrstis, dancing poses of hands and technique and conventions
Bhoja writes that bhava-vyakti in pictorial images depends on the rasas and rasa-drstis (eleven rasas, eighteen rasa-drstis) and that painting is based on dance and music
